title: onprem-control-ethos-and-sales-slate-healthcare-finserv-draft
content:
Purpose:
This is a short, pragmatic playbook for sales and solutions engineering when discussing Redwood Private (VPC / on-prem control plane) with regulated buyers in healthcare and financial services. Focus: control-plane language that reduces legal friction, technical heuristics for SRE/infra reviewers, and concise rebuttals to common procurement and security objections.

Audience/context:
- AE + SE pre-RFP discovery call, CISO/CPO intro, or compliance working session.
- Not a full security binder — use as talking points and an aide-memoire for early-stage pilots.

Topline positioning (elevator):
- "Redwood Private gives your teams a predictable inference runtime that keeps customer data and model execution inside your environment while letting our control plane orchestrate non-sensitive metadata from a hardened, auditable channel. It’s engineered for operational consistency — same API surface you get in hosted mode but with controls that align to regulated procurement."

Key messages to land early:
1) Data residency and exec boundary: We never require customer PII or PHI to be exported. Model inputs and outputs can be pinned to your VPC or on-prem nodes; the Redwood control plane operates on orchestration-level metadata only (job ids, status, telemetry IDs) — explain what metadata looks like.
2) Control plane minimalism: Our control plane is designed to be thin and replaceable — it handles scheduling, image/version pointers, and policy flags. It does NOT retain payloads by default and supports customer-managed encryption keys for any transit or storage hooks.
3) Auditability & proof: Ship examples of audit logs (sample schema), explain tamper-evident retention, and point to available SOC2 / FedRAMP artifacts where applicable in enterprise contracts.
4) Gradual ramp / pilot-first approach: Start with a read-only audit pilot (no PII allowed), then a small closed-loop pilot with synthetic or de-identified data, then expand to live workloads with agreed retention policies.

Technical talk-tracks (for SEs) — quick heuristics:
- Networking: We support private peering, VPC endpoints, and mutual TLS. For air-gapped customers we can run an on-prem control plane image with an ops-runbook for software delivery.
- Key management: Integrates with KMS (AWS/GCP/Azure) or HSM; customer retains root keys. Outline: we use envelope encryption for any cached artifacts.
- Failover and fallback: Canary routing and local fallback to a smaller model variant are available — call out SLO impact and how we surface traces in Console.
- Logging and PII: By default, request payloads are not persisted in central logs. If requested for debugging, logs can be written to customer S3/GCS bucket with restricted retention and role bindings.

Common objections + crisp rebuttals (copy-paste friendly):
- "We can’t have any outbound connections to vendor control planes."
  Rebuttal: "We offer a private control plane option that can be deployed into your VPC (air-gapped pattern available). For orchestration-only setups we can do signed manifests via an approved bastion with offline sync; we’ll run the delivery model from your infra entirely."

- "Vendor could change model behavior / leak data."
  Rebuttal: "Model binaries and weights run in your environment — there’s no exfil of model artifacts. The control plane only references image digests and version tags. Behavior changes require a signed rollout from your release policy or our mutually agreed A/B rollouts."

- "How do you handle subpoenas/regulatory requests?"
  Rebuttal: "We provide a documented legal process and will only process requests per contractually agreed terms — customers control data residency and can require us to route legal notices through their designated channel. We also offer contract language for narrow-scope mutual notification and transparency."

- "We need high-assurance attestation for supply-chain / SBOM."
  Rebuttal: "We provide SBOMs for agent images, CI provenance, and a reproducible build pipeline. For high-assurance buyers we support reproducible image verification and can integrate with your image-signing workflow."

Competitive snapshot — quick callouts to use in discovery
(keep short; avoid getting into feature-by-feature rabbit hole)
- Large cloud providers: Strengths — deep compliance programs and integrated cloud services. Weakness — inconsistent inference economics, less opinionated inference runtime. Ask: "Do you need high-control inference with ops-focused tooling?"
- Open-source runtimes (self-host): Strengths — flexibility, no vendor lock-in. Weakness — build-and-operate burden for batching, KV cache, and SLOs at scale. Ask: "Do you have the runway to maintain a production inference stack?"
- Other inference vendors (managed): Strengths — turnkey hosting. Weakness — limited private deployment options or high lift for air-gapped. Position: Redwood blends managed ergonomics with deployability into customer infra.

Pilot checklist (what to agree in week 0):
- Scope: workload type, approximate QPS, average and 95th token lengths
- Data handling: allowed data class (synthetic/PII/no-PII), retention window, debug-log policy
- Networking & keys: VPC/subnet CIDRs, firewall rules, KMS ARN or HSM contact
- SLA targets for pilot: latency p50/p95 goals, error budget thresholds, fallback paths
- Rollout stops: clear go/no-go criteria and acceptance tests (semantic quality, latency, cost per token)

Two short scripts for customer meetings (pick one):
- CISO opener: "We’re here to align on the compliance envelope. Tell me about the highest-value inference workloads you’d run and the controls that would make you comfortable to pilot—data residency, key control, and a proof-of-concept retention policy are usually the right levers."
- Engineering opener: "Let’s walk through an end-to-end request — where it enters your network, how it’s routed to an inference node, and what observability you need on token-level latency. We’ll map that to our recommended instance types and caching configuration."

Sample negotiation asks for contract stage:
- We ask for a 3-month pilot with limited SLA and a product SLA that kicks in after production acceptance.
- Require customer-located logs for debugging, vendor access only with break-glass logged and time-limited keys.
- Include a clause for source-of-truth image digests and a monthly SBOM delivery for agent images.

Open questions / ops risks to follow up with Eng:
- Clearer articulation for what constitutes "orchestration metadata" in our logging schema (SEs want examples).
- Standard playbook for offline air-gapped upgrades — needs runbook + security approval checklist.
- Template language for KMS/HSM integration SLAs and failure modes (rotation, revocation).

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Draft short appendix with three sample audit log snippets and anonymized screenshots of Console showing rollouts + audit event timeline.
- Get legal to sign off on the pilot contract bullets above (sample contract language).
- Sync with Applied ML on recommended quantization/variant mix for HPC vs latency-critical instances — include a simple cost/latency tradeoff table.

Why this is different from the usual doc stash:
- It’s intentionally conversational and executable for AEs/SEs during discovery — not a compliance binder or full security review pack. Use it to move buyers from discovery to a small pilot with clear asks and risk controls.
